title: Making of the Constitution
summary: How the Constitution came about: British-era Acts, the Constituent Assembly, sources, Schedules and the parliamentary system.

subcards.title: Historical background (1773–1947)
subcards.summary: How British Acts from 1773 to 1947 built the base of our Constitution.

sections.heading: Company rule (1773–1858): Regulating Act to Charter Act 1853

blocks.text: From 1773 the British Parliament began to control the East India Company (the 'Company') by passing Acts. Each Act below added one more piece of our later system of government.

blocks.title: Acts of the Company period
head: Act (year)
Main provisions
Why it matters for exams
rows: Governor of Bengal became 'Governor-General of Bengal' (first: Warren Hastings), helped by an Executive Council of 4 members. Governors of Bombay and Madras made subordinate to him. Supreme Court at Calcutta set up in 1774 (1 Chief Justice and 3 other judges). Company servants banned from private trade and from taking gifts or bribes. Court of Directors (the Company's governing body) had to report its revenue, civil and military affairs to the British Government.

First step by the British Government to control the Company. First recognition of the Company's political and administrative work. Laid the foundation of central administration in India. It did NOT abolish the Court of Directors.

Governor-General, Council and Company servants freed from the Supreme Court's jurisdiction for official acts. Revenue matters kept out of the Supreme Court. Court to apply personal law (Hindu law for Hindus, Muslim law for Muslims).
Corrected the defects of the 1773 Act.

Separated the Company's commercial work from its political work. Court of Directors kept commercial affairs; a new Board of Control managed political affairs. This was called 'double government' (two bodies in England sharing control of India). Governor-General's council reduced from 4 to 3 members.

Company territories called 'British possessions in India' for the first time. British Government got supreme control over the Company's affairs (direct control of Indian affairs). Court of Directors was NOT abolished.
Lord Cornwallis (Governor-General of Bengal) got power to override his council in special cases, and was also made Commander-in-Chief.

The power to override the council was extended to all later Governor-Generals and Governors. Governor-General's control over Bombay and Madras increased. Company's trade monopoly in India extended for 20 more years. Board of Control members to be paid from Indian revenues.
Remember: extended the monopoly; did not end it.

Ended the Company's trade monopoly in India (trade opened to all British merchants), except trade in tea and trade with China. Asserted the British Crown's sovereignty (supreme authority) over the Company's Indian territories. Allowed Christian missionaries to come to India. Provided for spreading western education (₹1 lakh a year for education). Allowed local governments to tax persons and punish non-payment.
Monopoly ended in 1813, but the Company remained a trader in tea and China trade until 1833.

Governor-General of Bengal became Governor-General of India, with all civil and military powers (first: Lord William Bentinck). Governors of Bombay and Madras lost their law-making powers. Laws made earlier were called 'Regulations'; laws made now were called 'Acts'. Ended the Company's commercial activities, so it became a purely administrative body. Tried to start open competition for civil servants and said Indians should not be barred from any post, but the Court of Directors opposed it and it did not take effect. Directed the Government of India to take steps to abolish slavery. A Law Commission was set up under it (first Law Commission, 1834, chaired by Lord Macaulay).
Final step towards centralisation. For the first time the 'Government of India' had authority over all British territory in India.

Separated, for the first time, the legislative and executive functions of the Governor-General's council: 6 new members called legislative councillors were added, forming the Indian (Central) Legislative Council, which worked like a mini-Parliament. Introduced open competition to recruit civil servants, so the covenanted (higher) civil service opened to Indians; Macaulay Committee appointed in 1854. Company kept Indian territories 'in trust' for the Crown, but no time period was fixed. Of the 6 new members, 4 were appointed by the local governments of Madras, Bombay, Bengal and Agra.

Last Charter Act (series 1793–1853). First local representation in the Central Legislative Council. The 4 provincial members were APPOINTED by governments, not elected Indians. No fixed period meant Parliament could end Company rule any time.

sections.heading: Crown rule begins: Act of 1858 and the Indian Councils Acts (1861, 1892, 1909)

blocks.title: Acts from 1858 to 1909
head: Act (year)
Main provisions
Why it matters for exams
rows: Government of India Act (1858) — 'Act for the Good Government of India'

Passed after the Revolt of 1857. Abolished the East India Company and transferred government, territories and revenues of India to the British Crown. Governor-General of India renamed Viceroy of India (first: Lord Canning). Ended double government by abolishing the Board of Control and the Court of Directors. Created a new office, the Secretary of State for India — a member of the British Cabinet, responsible to the British Parliament. Created a 15-member advisory Council of India to help him; he was its chairman. The Secretary of State-in-Council (the Secretary of State together with his council) was made a legal body that could sue and be sued in courts.

Company rule ended; Crown rule began. It did NOT separate legislative and executive functions (that was 1853) and did NOT create a Board of Control (that was 1784). It mainly improved the control machinery in England, not the system inside India.

Beginning of representative institutions: the Viceroy could nominate Indians as non-official members of his enlarged council. In 1862 Lord Canning nominated 3 Indians: the Raja of Benaras, the Maharaja of Patiala and Sir Dinkar Rao. Restored law-making powers to Bombay and Madras (start of decentralisation, also called legislative devolution). New legislative councils for Bengal (1862), North-Western Provinces (1886) and Punjab (1897). Gave legal recognition to the 'portfolio' system started by Lord Canning in 1859 (one council member in charge of one or more departments). The Viceroy could issue ordinances (temporary laws made by the executive) in an emergency without the council's consent. An ordinance lasted 6 months.
Reversed the centralisation that began in 1773 and peaked in 1833. The executive council was NOT made responsible to the legislature.
Under it, High Courts were set up at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras.
See the Supreme Court and High Courts topic for details.

Increased additional (non-official) members, but kept an official majority. Councils could discuss the budget (but not vote on it) and ask questions to the executive. Some non-official members were nominated on the recommendation of bodies such as provincial councils, the Bengal Chamber of Commerce, district boards, municipalities, universities and zamindars.

This was a limited and indirect use of election. The word 'election' was not used — it was called 'nomination on recommendation'. So: an indirect representative element inside a nomination system. The budget system itself began in 1860.

Lord Morley was the Secretary of State for India; Lord Minto was the Viceroy. Central Legislative Council members raised from 16 to 60. Central council kept an official majority; provincial councils could have a non-official majority. Members could ask supplementary questions and move resolutions on the budget. For the first time Indians joined the executive councils of the Viceroy and Governors: Satyendra Prasad Sinha became the first Indian in the Viceroy's Executive Council (Law Member). Introduced 'separate electorate' for Muslims: Muslim members elected only by Muslim voters. Separate representation also for presidency corporations, chambers of commerce, universities and zamindars.

It 'legalised communalism'. Lord Minto is called the 'Father of Communal Electorate'. A non-official majority did not mean an elected majority (non-officials could be nominated). It did NOT bring dyarchy.

sections.heading: Government of India Act 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms)

blocks.title: Background
items: 20 August 1917: the British Government declared for the first time that its aim was the gradual introduction of responsible government in India (Montagu's declaration).
Montagu was the Secretary of State for India; Lord Chelmsford was the Viceroy.
It was an Act of the British (UK) Parliament. It came into force in 1921; the new Council of State and Legislative Assembly were inaugurated in 1921.

blocks.title: Main features
head: Feature
What it means
rows: All subjects were divided into central and provincial lists by the 'Devolution Rules' (rules that handed some subjects over to the provinces). Each legislature made laws on its own list. This clearly defined the jurisdiction of the central and provincial governments, but the system stayed centralised and unitary.

Provincial subjects were split into 'transferred' and 'reserved'. Transferred subjects: run by the Governor with ministers responsible to the legislative council. Reserved subjects: run by the Governor and his executive council, not responsible to the legislature. The word comes from the Greek 'di-arche', meaning double rule. The experiment largely failed.

For the first time, two Houses at the Centre (bicameralism). Upper House: Council of State (60 members, 5-year term). Lower House: Legislative Assembly (145 members, 3-year term). Most members of both Houses were directly elected.
Indians in the Viceroy's Executive Council
3 of the 6 members (other than the Commander-in-Chief) had to be Indians.
Separate electorates extended to Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians and Europeans.
Right to vote only for a few people, based on property, tax or other qualifications. (It did not give the vote to all women above 21.)
High Commissioner for India in London
New office; took over some functions of the Secretary of State.
Provided for under Section 96(C) of the Act. A Central Public Service Commission was set up in 1926 (1 October 1926) on the recommendation of the Lee Commission (1923–24).
For the first time provincial budgets were separated from the Central budget (not merged).
A commission was to review the Act 10 years after it came into force (this became the Simon Commission).
Inaugurated in 1921; 120 members; headed by the Viceroy.

sections.heading: From Simon Commission to the Poona Pact (1927–1932)

items.what: Commonwealth of India Bill
items.detail: Drafted by the National Convention (Tej Bahadur Sapru), revised under Annie Besant; presented in the British House of Commons by George Lansbury (December 1925). Listed 7 fundamental rights, including free elementary education. It was not passed.

items.what: Simon Commission appointed
items.detail: 7 members, chairman Sir John Simon; appointed 2 years before schedule. All members were British, so all Indian parties boycotted it.

items.what: Nehru Report
items.detail: Committee headed by Motilal Nehru drafted a constitution for India.

items.what: Simon Commission report
items.detail: Recommended: abolish dyarchy, extend responsible government in provinces, a federation of British India and princely states, continue communal electorates.

items.what: Three Round Table Conferences in London
items.detail: Congress did not attend the First. After the Gandhi–Irwin Pact, Gandhi represented Congress at the Second (1931). Third in 1932. Then a White Paper went to a Joint Select Committee of the British Parliament; its proposals became the 1935 Act.

items.what: Karachi session of Congress
items.detail: Presided over by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel. Passed the resolution on Fundamental Rights and economic policy — beyond civil freedoms it included aims like a living wage and free primary education.

items.what: Communal Award
items.detail: By British Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald. Continued separate electorates for Muslims, Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians and Europeans, and extended them to the depressed classes (Scheduled Castes).

items.what: Poona Pact
items.detail: Gandhi fasted in Yerawada Jail (Poona). Agreement between Congress and Dr B.R. Ambedkar: Hindus (including the depressed classes) kept voting together in one joint electorate, but some seats were reserved for the depressed classes. Britain accepted it; it was included in the 1935 Act.

blocks.title: Other facts in this period
items: Lord Mayo's Resolution on financial decentralisation was in 1870 — earlier than the Simon Commission (1930), the 1935 Act and the Constituent Assembly.
Dadabhai Naoroji was the first Indian elected to the British House of Commons (1892).

sections.heading: Government of India Act 1935

blocks.text: A long, detailed Act: 321 Sections and 10 Schedules. It was the second milestone towards fully responsible government. It was based on federation and a parliamentary system.

blocks.title: Main features
head: Feature
Details
rows: Provinces and princely states as units. Three lists: Federal List (59 items), Provincial List (54 items), Concurrent List (36 items). The federation NEVER came into being because the princely states (whose joining was voluntary) did not join.

Given to the Governor-General (Viceroy) — not to the Federal or Provincial legislature. In his discretion he could, by public notification, allow the Federal or a Provincial legislature to make a law on a matter not in any list.

Abolished dyarchy in the provinces. Provinces became autonomous units in their own fields, with responsible governments (Governor to act on advice of ministers responsible to the provincial legislature). Came into effect in 1937; discontinued in 1939.
Federal subjects split into reserved and transferred. This provision NEVER came into operation, because the federation itself never began.
Bengal, Bombay, Madras, Bihar, Assam and United Provinces got a legislative council (upper house) and legislative assembly (lower house).
Council of State 260 members; Federal Assembly 375 members (never formed, as the federation did not begin).

Communal electorates and weightage (extra seats beyond a community's population share) were extended further. Some general seats reserved for depressed classes (from the Poona Pact). Special representation for women and labour.
The 1858 Council of India ended; the Secretary of State got a team of advisers.
About 14% of the total population got the right to vote.
Provided for, to control currency and credit. (The Reserve Bank of India itself was set up under its own RBI Act 1934 and began work in 1935.)
A Federal Public Service Commission, a Provincial Public Service Commission for each province, and a Joint Public Service Commission for two or more provinces.
Set up in 1937. It was not the final court — appeals still went to the Privy Council in London.
Burma separated from India. Two new provinces: Orissa and Sind. Safeguards for minorities. Federal Railway Authority. Auditor-General of India.

Constitution of India

sections.heading: Road to independence (1940–1947) and the Indian Independence Act

blocks.title: From the August Offer to 15 August 1947

items.what: Congress first officially demands a Constituent Assembly
items.detail: The idea was first given by M.N. Roy in 1934. See the Constituent Assembly card (mk-ca).

items.what: August Offer
items.detail: By Viceroy Linlithgow. Promised an expanded Viceroy's Executive Council and a constitution-making body after the war. Accepted the Constituent Assembly demand in principle.

items.what: Cripps Proposals
items.detail: Sir Stafford Cripps, a British Cabinet member. Constituent Assembly after the war: members ELECTED by provincial assemblies and NOMINATED by princely states. Any province not accepting the new constitution could sign a separate agreement with Britain. Rejected by Congress and the Muslim League.

items.what: Wavell Plan and Simla Conference
items.detail: By Viceroy Lord Wavell (June 1945). Plan to reconstitute the Viceroy's Executive Council so that all members except the Viceroy and the Commander-in-Chief would be Indians (the Commander-in-Chief kept the War portfolio). The Simla Conference held to discuss it failed.

items.what: Cabinet Mission Plan
items.detail: Rejected Pakistan (two Constituent Assemblies). Proposed a Union handling foreign affairs, defence and communications; grouping of provinces; an interim government in which all portfolios, including War, would be held by Indian leaders; and a scheme for the Constituent Assembly. The Constituent Assembly was formed (November 1946) under this plan. It did NOT create two independent states.

items.what: Interim Government formed
items.detail: Headed by Jawaharlal Nehru as Vice-President of the Viceroy's Executive Council (the Viceroy stayed head). All portfolios, including Defence (Baldev Singh), were held by Indians.

items.what: Attlee's statement
items.detail: British Prime Minister Clement Attlee announced that British rule would end by 30 June 1948.

items.what: Mountbatten Plan
items.detail: Partition plan by Viceroy Lord Mountbatten; accepted by Congress and the Muslim League. Date of transfer was advanced to 15 August 1947 (June 1948 was not kept).

items.what: Indian Independence Bill
items.detail: Introduced on 4 July; got Royal Assent (the King's formal approval) on 18 July — about 15 days. Act came into force on 15 August 1947. Clement Attlee was the British Prime Minister.

blocks.title: Indian Independence Act 1947 — features
head: Feature
Details
rows: India independent from 15 August 1947. Two dominions (self-governing countries under the British Crown), India and Pakistan, with the right to leave the British Commonwealth.
Viceroy's office abolished. Each dominion got a Governor-General appointed by the British King on the advice of the dominion cabinet.
Could frame any constitution and repeal any British Act, even this Act. It also became the law-making body (Parliament of the dominion). See the Constituent Assembly card (mk-ca).

Each dominion and its provinces were governed by the Government of India Act 1935 (with modifications) until the new Constitution — so from 1947 to 26 January 1950 India was run under the adapted 1935 Act.

Office abolished; functions went to the Secretary of State for Commonwealth Affairs. Appointments to civil services and reservation of posts by him stopped; officers appointed before 15 August 1947 kept all their benefits.
British paramountcy (overlordship) over them lapsed. They were free to join India or Pakistan, or remain independent.
Lost the right to veto bills or reserve them for his approval (this right went to the Governor-General). Title 'Emperor of India' dropped.
Governor-General and provincial Governors became constitutional (nominal) heads, acting on the advice of councils of ministers — so responsible government was complete.
It was an Act without a constitution — it did not give India a ready-made constitution.

blocks.title: After 15 August 1947
items: Lord Mountbatten became the first Governor-General of free India; he (the Governor-General) swore in Jawaharlal Nehru as the first Prime Minister.
British sovereignty did NOT continue in free India, although the British King did appoint the Governor-General.

sections.heading: Exam traps

items: The post of Governor-General of India was created by the Charter Act 1833 (Bentinck), not 1773 (that was Governor-General of Bengal) and not 1858 (that made him Viceroy).
Dyarchy in provinces came in 1919. The 1935 Act ABOLISHED provincial dyarchy and proposed dyarchy at the Centre (never worked).
Two Houses (bicameralism) at the Centre came in 1919; in 6 provinces, in 1935.
1935 Act residuary powers went to the Governor-General, not the Federal Legislature.
1935 lists: Federal 59, Provincial 54, Concurrent 36. No 'Union List' in 1935.
The 1813 Act ended the trade monopoly (except tea and trade with China); the 1833 Act ended all commercial activity.
Principle of election began in 1892 (indirect); separate electorate in 1909 (Minto); extended to Sikhs and others in 1919; to depressed classes by the Communal Award 1932.

Cripps Proposals (1942): members from the provinces were to be ELECTED by the provincial assemblies, not nominated; only the princely states were to nominate their members. Cabinet Mission (1946) rejected the demand for Pakistan.

at_a_glance: 389 seats planned in 1946; reduced to 299 after Partition (1947)
Set up 29 August 1947; 7 members; chairman Dr. B.R. Ambedkar

sections.heading: How the demand came and how the Assembly was formed

items.what: M.N. Roy, a pioneer of the communist movement in India, first put forward the idea of a Constituent Assembly for India.
items.detail: Some exam papers give the option 'Swaraj Party in 1934' instead of M.N. Roy — if M.N. Roy is not among the options, choose the 1934 option.

items.what: Indian National Congress (INC) officially demanded a Constituent Assembly for the first time.
Jawaharlal Nehru, speaking for the INC, declared that the Constitution of free India must be framed, without outside interference, by a Constituent Assembly elected on the basis of adult franchise.
INC passed a resolution repeating this demand.
August Offer: the British Government accepted the demand in principle (for the first time).

Cripps Proposals: a British plan for framing a Constitution for India after World War II. The Muslim League rejected it because it wanted India divided into two, with two separate Constituent Assemblies.
Cabinet Mission Plan: rejected the idea of two Assemblies and gave the scheme under which the Constituent Assembly was actually formed (November 1946).
items.detail: The Cabinet Mission had three members — Lord Pethick-Lawrence, Sir Stafford Cripps and A.V. Alexander. It arrived in India on 24 March 1946 and published its plan on 16 May 1946.

A partly elected, partly nominated body; the provincial assemblies themselves were elected on a limited franchise (only people with tax, property or similar qualifications could vote, under the Government of India Act, 1935)

blocks.title: Objectives Resolution
head: Aspect
Fact
rows: Laid down the basic ideas and philosophy of the Constitution: India an Independent Sovereign Republic; a Union of all territories; all power comes from the people; justice, equality and freedoms for all; safeguards for minorities, backward and tribal areas
A modified version of it is our present Preamble

blocks.text: Text and meaning of the Preamble → see Preamble

blocks.title: Three changes made by the Indian Independence Act, 1947
head: Change
What it meant
rows: The Assembly could frame any Constitution it liked and could cancel or change any British law relating to India

It got two jobs: making the Constitution AND making ordinary laws. The two were done on separate days. As the law-making body (Dominion Legislature, the first Parliament of free India) it was chaired by G.V. Mavalankar; as the Constitution-making body, by Dr. Rajendra Prasad. Both jobs went on till 26 November 1949
Muslim League members from areas in Pakistan withdrew

head: Source
What it did
rows: Drafted by the National Convention, which was chaired by Tej Bahadur Sapru, with Annie Besant as a leading figure behind the Bill. It was presented in the British House of Commons by George Lansbury (Labour MP) in December 1925. Listed seven fundamental rights, including free elementary education
Suggested dividing rights into two kinds: justiciable (can be enforced in a court) and non-justiciable (cannot be enforced in a court)

Recommended dividing individual rights into justiciable (court-enforceable) and non-justiciable ones. The Drafting Committee accepted this, so Fundamental Rights went into Part III and Directive Principles into Part IV
Its Part I listed rights that could be enforced, with a guaranteed right to go to the Supreme Court for them. Its Part II listed principles of state policy that courts could NOT enforce

sections.heading: Drafting and enactment of the Constitution

items.what: Congress Experts Committee (chairman Nehru) set up to prepare material for the Assembly; it also drafted a resolution close to the Objectives Resolution.
Drafting Committee set up.
First draft published (315 Articles and 8 Schedules). People got eight months to discuss it and suggest amendments.
Second draft published, after public comments.
Ambedkar introduced the final draft in the Assembly. This began the First Reading (general discussion), which lasted five days, till 9 November 1948.
Second Reading, in which the draft was discussed clause by clause. 7,653 amendments were proposed; 2,473 were actually discussed.
Third Reading began. Ambedkar moved: 'the Constitution as settled by the Assembly be passed'.
Motion declared passed — Constitution ADOPTED. Of 299 members, 284 were present and signed. This is the date in the Preamble ('adopted, enacted and given to ourselves').
Final session: members signed the Constitution; National Anthem and National Song adopted; Rajendra Prasad elected first President of India.
Rest of the Constitution came into force — the 'date of commencement', celebrated as Republic Day.

blocks.title: More about the 1935 Act as a source
items: About 250 provisions of the 1935 Act were included; more than half of the Constitution is the same as or close to that Act.

The 1935 Act first gave an all-India federal structure with provincial autonomy and divided law-making powers between the Centre and the provinces in three lists. The Seventh Schedule's three lists come from it.

Directive Principles are like the 'Instrument of Instructions' (orders the British Government gave to the Governor-General and Governors) under the 1935 Act. Ambedkar said Directive Principles are 'merely another name' for them.
The 1935 Act's All-India Federation never came into being, because the princely states, whose joining was voluntary, did not join it. Provincial autonomy did start in 1937.

blocks.text: Borrowing is not copying: the US Bill of Rights inspired our Fundamental Rights, but our list and its limits are different from the American ones.

sections.heading: Kinds of constitutions

blocks.text: A constitution is the set of basic written rules that everyone in a country accepts. It sets up the organs of government, gives their powers and relations, and is the supreme law of the land.

blocks.title: Ways to classify constitutions
head: Basis
Types
Meaning
Examples
rows: Evolved: grows slowly from customs, conventions and court decisions. Enacted: deliberately framed by a special body (like a constituent assembly) at a fixed time
Written: in a document or a set of documents (codified). Unwritten (uncodified): spread across conventions, statutes, charters and court decisions
Written: USA, Canada, Japan, France, Germany, India. Unwritten: UK, New Zealand, Israel
Rigid: needs a special procedure to amend. Flexible: amended like an ordinary law
Rigid: USA, Australia, Switzerland. Flexible: UK, New Zealand. India: a mix of both

Federal: the constitution itself divides powers between national and regional governments. Unitary: all power with the national government, which may delegate some to regions and take it back by ordinary law
Federal: USA, Switzerland, Australia, Canada, Russia, Brazil, Argentina, Nigeria, India. Unitary: UK, France, Japan, China, Italy, Norway, Sweden, Sri Lanka
Parliamentary: executive answerable to the legislature. Presidential: executive separate from the legislature, with a fixed term
Parliamentary: Britain, Japan, Canada, India. Presidential: USA

blocks.title: Key clarifications
items: An uncodified (unwritten) constitution can still contain written statutes (Acts of Parliament). The UK has many.
A flexible constitution is not always unwritten. The two ideas answer different questions: 'written or unwritten' is about its form, while 'rigid or flexible' is about how easy it is to amend.
Constitutional conventions are rules followed by long practice but not enforced by courts. Example: the British monarch always gives assent to Bills passed by Parliament.
A unitary state may have an unwritten constitution (Britain) or a written one (France), and two Houses (Britain) or one House (China). A federation needs a written, supreme and rigid constitution.
New Zealand's Constitution Act 1986 is only one of its constitutional documents; it is not a full codified constitution.
Sri Lanka's Constitution itself declares the republic a 'unitary State'.

Thinkers: Aristotle studied about 158 constitutions and classified them; James Bryce gave the rigid–flexible classification; A.V. Dicey explained rule of law and conventions of the constitution; Montesquieu gave separation of powers (The Spirit of Laws).

blocks.title: 'Union of States' (Article 1)
items: The word 'Federation' is not used anywhere in the Constitution.
Ambedkar explained why 'Union' was used: (1) the Indian federation is not the result of an agreement among the states, and (2) no state has the right to secede (leave) from it.
Ambedkar, moving the Draft on 4 November 1948: the Constitution 'could be both unitary as well as federal according to the requirements of time and circumstances'.
So exams describe India as quasi-federal, or 'unitary with federal features', not 'truly federal'.

blocks.title: Indian federation follows the Canadian model, not the American

Uses the term 'Union' (Canada is also called a Union).

Residuary powers (subjects not in any list) lie with the Centre, as in Canada. In the USA they lie with the states.

sections.heading: Parliamentary system and judicial review

blocks.title: Parliamentary system (British, 'Westminster' model)
items: Based on co-operation between the legislature and the executive; the presidential system is based on separation of powers.
Applies at the Centre and in the states.

Features: a nominal (name-only) head, the President, and a real executive, the Prime Minister and ministers; majority party rule; collective responsibility (all ministers answer together to the legislature); ministers must be members of the legislature; leadership of the Prime Minister or Chief Minister; power to dissolve (end early) the Lok Sabha or the state Assembly.
Because ministers sit in Parliament, India does NOT follow strict US-style separation of powers.

blocks.title: India vs Britain vs USA
head: Aspect
India
Britain / USA
rows: Not sovereign; limited by the Constitution and judicial review
Britain: Parliament is sovereign, and courts cannot strike down its Acts
Narrower: Art 21 uses 'procedure established by law', so courts mainly check whether a valid law and its procedure were followed
USA: wider, uses 'due process of law', so courts also check whether the law itself is fair. This is called judicial supremacy (courts have the final word)

blocks.title: Synthesis (balance) of parliamentary sovereignty and judicial supremacy
items: The Supreme Court can declare laws of Parliament unconstitutional (judicial review).
Parliament can amend most of the Constitution (constituent power), but not its basic structure.

A case that raises a substantial (important) question about the meaning of the Constitution, such as the validity of a constitutional amendment, is heard by a Constitution Bench of at least five judges (Art 145(3)).
Judicial review is NOT a British feature; it came from the USA.

Three kinds: National Emergency (Art 352); President's Rule in a state (Art 356 and Art 365); Financial Emergency (Art 360). During an Emergency the federal system works like a unitary one, without any amendment of the Constitution

blocks.note: All these are created by the Constitution itself, not by an executive order or ordinary law. UPSC was in the original Constitution; 'secular', Fundamental Duties and the 'basic structure' idea were not (basic structure comes from a 1973 court judgment, not the text).

blocks.title: Other features
items: Integrated and independent judiciary: one system of courts (Supreme Court, then High Courts, then subordinate courts) enforces both central and state laws, unlike the USA's two separate systems.

Secular state: no official religion; 'secular' added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment (1976); India follows positive secularism (equal respect for all religions). A 'religious state' is NOT a feature.
Universal adult franchise: every citizen aged 18 or above can vote; age cut from 21 to 18 by the 61st Amendment (1988).

Single citizenship: India has a dual polity (Centre and states) but only one citizenship. The USA has dual citizenship (of the country and of the state). The Citizenship Act, 1955 also provides only single citizenship, so dual citizenship is not allowed.
Liberal constitution: it guarantees Fundamental Rights to individuals.
Three-tier government: Panchayats (73rd Amendment, 1992) and Municipalities (74th Amendment, 1992).
Co-operative societies: the 97th Amendment (2011) made forming co-operative societies a Fundamental Right in Art 19, added a new Directive Principle in Art 43B, and added a new Part IXB.
The Constitution is supreme. It does not make the judiciary supreme over it.

The Governor can, by public notification, direct that an Act of Parliament or the State Legislature shall not apply to a Scheduled Area, or apply with changes.
The Governor can make regulations (after consulting the Tribes Advisory Council) to stop transfer of tribal land and control money-lending. These need the President's assent.

blocks.title: Seventh Schedule — the three Lists
items: There are three Lists (Art 246): List I is the Union List, List II is the State List and List III is the Concurrent List. Not two, not four.
Union List: 98 subjects now (97 originally) — matters of national importance such as defence and foreign affairs.
State List: 59 subjects now (66 originally) — for example police and public order, so preventing and investigating crime is mainly the States' duty.
Concurrent List: 52 subjects now (47 originally).
Original numbers, in the order Union, State, Concurrent: 97, 66, 47.
The three-list scheme came from the Government of India Act, 1935 (which had federal, provincial and concurrent lists). The Concurrent List idea is also credited to Australia.
Changing any List in the Seventh Schedule needs a special majority of Parliament and approval (ratification) by the Legislatures of half the States.

blocks.title: Basics
items: Added by the 1st Amendment Act, 1951, when Jawaharlal Nehru was Prime Minister, together with Art 31A and Art 31B.
Purpose: protect land reform and zamindari-abolition laws from being struck down for violating Fundamental Rights.

State laws in it are mostly land reform laws, while the laws of Parliament in it deal with other matters. So the Ninth Schedule is not limited to land reform.
Only Parliament can place a law in it, by a constitutional amendment. A State Act or a Governor's assent cannot do it, and no law enters it automatically.

subcards.title: Parliamentary System
subcards.summary: Why India's government is answerable to Parliament, and how it differs from US and UK.
at_a_glance: The government (executive) is answerable to the legislature, mainly the Lok Sabha
Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister (Centre) or Chief Minister (State)
Cabinet government, responsible government, Westminster model
British parliamentary system, but India did not copy it exactly
Ambedkar: the framers chose a government that is more answerable (more responsibility) over one that is harder to remove (more stability)

sections.heading: What a parliamentary system is

items: Governments are classified as parliamentary or presidential by looking at how the executive (the government that runs the country) is related to the legislature (Parliament).
Parliamentary system: the executive is responsible (answerable) to the legislature for its policies and acts, and can be removed by it.
Presidential system: the executive is NOT responsible to the legislature and has a fixed term that the legislature cannot cut short (except by impeachment).

India's Constitution sets up a parliamentary government at BOTH the Centre and the States. The Preamble calls India a sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic, and its system of government is parliamentary.
Other names: 'cabinet government', 'responsible government' and 'Westminster model' (named after Westminster, the place in London where the British Parliament sits and where this system began).
The parliamentary system is also found in Britain, Japan and Canada. The presidential system is found in the USA, Brazil, Russia and Sri Lanka.
The presidential system is also called the non-responsible system (the executive is not answerable to the legislature), the non-parliamentary system or the fixed-executive system.
Ivor Jennings called it the 'cabinet system' because the cabinet is the centre (nucleus) of power.
The Indian Parliament is mainly modelled on the British Parliament. The cabinet system is one of the features India borrowed from Britain.

blocks.title: Articles that create the parliamentary system
head: Article
What it says
rows: There shall be a Council of Ministers, headed by the Prime Minister, to aid and advise the President. The President must act on this advice.
The President appoints the Prime Minister. The President appoints the other ministers on the Prime Minister's advice.
The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible (answerable as one team) to the Lok Sabha. This is the foundation of the parliamentary system.
A person who is not a member of Parliament can be made a minister. But if he does not become a member of either House within six consecutive months, he stops being a minister.
The Prime Minister has a duty to give information to the President (about decisions of the Council of Ministers and proposals for laws).
The President can dissolve the Lok Sabha (end it before its term, leading to fresh elections). In practice, he does this on the Prime Minister's advice.
There shall be a Council of Ministers, headed by the Chief Minister, to aid and advise the Governor.
The State Council of Ministers is collectively responsible (answerable as one team) to the Legislative Assembly of the State.
blocks.note: The 42nd Amendment (1976) made the ministers' advice binding on the President. The 44th Amendment (1978) allowed the President to send the advice back once for reconsideration. But he must act on the advice given after reconsideration.

blocks.title: Union and State counterparts
head: Union level
State level

Chief Minister: head of the State Council of Ministers

sections.heading: Eight features of parliamentary government in India

head: Feature
Meaning
How it works in India
rows: There are two executives: one is head in name only, and the other holds the real power.

The President is the nominal executive: the de jure (by law) or titular (in title only) head, and the head of the State. The Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers are the real, de facto (in actual fact) executive, and the Prime Minister is the head of the government. The ministers' advice under Article 74 is binding on the President.
The party that wins a majority of seats in the Lok Sabha forms the government.
The President appoints the leader of the majority party as Prime Minister. If no single party has a majority, a coalition (a group of parties together) may be invited to form the government.
Ministers act as one team and 'swim and sink together' (they stay in office together or go out together). This is the bedrock (most basic) principle of the system.

Under Article 75, ministers are collectively responsible to Parliament in general and to the Lok Sabha in particular. The Lok Sabha can remove the whole ministry by passing a no-confidence motion. A minister who disagrees with a Cabinet decision must either support it or resign.
Ministers usually belong to the same party and share the same ideology (political ideas).
In a coalition government (ministers from several parties), ministers are bound by consensus (what all the parties have agreed upon).
Ministers are members of both the legislature (Parliament) and the executive (government) at the same time.
A minister must be a member of Parliament. A non-member can be a minister, but stops being a minister if he does not become a member within six consecutive months.
The Prime Minister is the leader of the whole system.
The Prime Minister is the leader of the Council of Ministers, the leader of Parliament and the leader of the ruling party.
The executive can get the lower House of the legislature dissolved (ended early).
The President can dissolve the Lok Sabha before its five-year term ends, on the Prime Minister's advice. Fresh elections are then held.
Ministers must not reveal the proceedings (discussions), policies or decisions of the government.

Before taking office, every Union minister takes an oath of secrecy. The President administers this oath (Article 75(4)). The form (exact words) of the oath is given in the Third Schedule of the Constitution.

blocks.title: Fusion of powers
items: In a parliamentary system, the legislature and the executive are joined together, not kept separate. This is called 'fusion of powers'.
A minister makes laws as a member of Parliament and also carries them out as part of the executive.
Even with fusion, the government stays accountable, because ministers sit in the legislature and remain answerable to the popular House (the directly elected Lok Sabha).
So India does NOT follow separation of powers in the American sense (where the three organs are kept fully apart). In India, the executive comes from the legislature.
Ministers can be members of EITHER House, but the Council of Ministers is responsible only to the Lok Sabha, not to the Rajya Sabha.

blocks.title: Checks between organs in India
head: Check
Instrument
rows: Judicial review (courts can strike down laws that violate the Constitution)
No-confidence motion, Question Hour, discussions and adjournment motion
The President dissolves the Lok Sabha on the advice of the ministers

blocks.title: Position of the President
items: The President is the head of the State, not the real head of the executive. Ambedkar said in the Constituent Assembly that the President's place in administration is 'that of a ceremonial device or a seal by which the nation's decisions are made known'.
The President's influence is persuasive (he can try to convince the ministers), not coercive (he cannot force them).

Walter Bagehot (The English Constitution, 1867) said the British monarch has three rights: the right to be consulted, the right to encourage and the right to warn. The Indian President is described as having the same three rights.
Many appointments are formally made by the President, but he makes them following the procedures laid down and on the advice of the ministers.
In 1947, the first Prime Minister, Jawaharlal Nehru, was sworn in by the Governor-General, Lord Mountbatten.

sections.heading: Presidential system and other models

blocks.title: Features of the American presidential system
items: One person, the President, is both the head of the State and the head of the government. This is called a single executive.

The US President is elected by an electoral college for a fixed term of four years. Congress (the US Parliament) cannot remove him by a no-confidence vote. It can remove him only by impeachment (a special removal process) for a grave unconstitutional act.

He governs with a cabinet, or a smaller 'Kitchen Cabinet' (an informal inner group of close advisers), made of non-elected departmental secretaries. They are only his advisers: he chooses them and they are responsible only to him.
The President and his secretaries are not answerable to Congress. They are not members of Congress and do not attend its sessions.
The US President cannot dissolve the House of Representatives (the lower House of Congress).
It is based on separation of powers: law-making (legislative), law-implementing (executive) and judicial powers are given to three separate, independent organs.
If the US President and Congress disagree, neither can remove the other. Both continue for their fixed terms.
Because power rests with one leader, the presidential system is called the system based on individual leadership.
The US Constitution is the oldest written national constitution still in force. This is a separate fact: it does not explain why the US has a presidential system.

blocks.title: Parliamentary vs presidential
head: Aspect
Parliamentary
Presidential
rows: Dual executive (one head in name, one with real power)
President and legislators are elected separately, each for a fixed term
Ministers are collectively answerable to the legislature
Executive is not answerable to the legislature
Political homogeneity (ministers from the same party)
Political homogeneity may not exist (secretaries may come from outside the party)
Double membership (ministers are also members of the legislature)
Single membership (secretaries are not members of Congress)
Harmony between legislature and executive. Responsible (answerable) government. Prevents despotism (rule by one all-powerful person). Wide representation.
Stable government. Definite policies. Based on separation of powers. Government by experts.
Unstable government. No continuity of policies. Against separation of powers. Government by amateurs (non-experts).
Conflict between legislature and executive. Non-responsible government. May lead to autocracy (one person's unchecked rule). Narrow representation.

Semi-presidential: a powerful, directly elected President works along with a Council of Ministers led by a Prime Minister, which is answerable to Parliament. Laxmikanth calls it 'quasi-presidential and quasi-parliamentary' (partly presidential, partly parliamentary).
Collegial (plural) executive: power is held by a group, the seven-member Federal Council, instead of one person

head: Form

Powers divided between the centre and the units

sections.heading: Merits, demerits and famous descriptions

blocks.title: Merits
head: Merit
Meaning
rows: This is the greatest advantage. The executive is part of the legislature, so there are fewer conflicts between the two.
This is the main advantage over the presidential system. Ministers are answerable to Parliament, which checks them through Question Hour, discussions, adjournment motion and no-confidence motion.
Power is with a group (the Council of Ministers), not with one person. This group can be removed by a no-confidence motion, so it cannot become a despot (all-powerful ruler).
If the ruling party loses its majority, the opposition can be invited to form the government without fresh elections. Jennings said: 'the leader of the opposition is the alternative prime minister'.
Ministers can be chosen from all sections of society and all regions.

blocks.title: Demerits
head: Demerit
Meaning
rows: The government can fall because of a no-confidence motion, defection (members leaving their party) or quarrels in a coalition. Examples: the governments of Morarji Desai, Charan Singh, V.P. Singh, Chandra Sekhar, Deve Gowda and I.K. Gujral.
A new ruling party often reverses the earlier government's policies. Examples: the Janata government in 1977, and the Congress again in 1980.

When the ruling party has an absolute majority, the cabinet can become autocratic (use almost unlimited power). H.J. Laski said this system gives the executive a chance for tyranny. Ramsay Muir used the phrase 'dictatorship of the cabinet'.
The legislature and the executive are fused (joined), not kept separate.
Ministers are usually not experts in their departments, and the Prime Minister has to choose ministers mainly from members of Parliament.
blocks.note: Exam point: 'responsible government' is a MERIT of the parliamentary system, not a demerit.

blocks.title: Who said what
head: Person
Description
rows: The Prime Minister is 'primus inter pares' (first among equals) and the 'keystone of the cabinet arch' (the central stone that holds the cabinet together).
The Prime Minister is 'a sun around which planets revolve' and 'the key-stone of the constitution'.
The Cabinet is 'the core of the British constitutional system'.
The Cabinet is 'a hyphen that joins, the buckle that binds' the executive and the legislature (it links the two together).
Called the British Cabinet a 'dictatorship of the cabinet' (in his book How Britain is Governed).
The British system has become 'prime ministerial government' (the Prime Minister dominates the cabinet). This description also fits India.
Gave the theory of separation of powers in his book The Spirit of Laws (1748).
Said the Draft Constitution 'preferred more responsibility to more stability'.
Said 'England is the mother of Parliaments' (speech at Birmingham, 18 January 1865).

sections.heading: Why India chose the parliamentary system

blocks.text: In the Constituent Assembly, K.T. Shah wanted the US-style presidential system. But the framers chose the British parliamentary system, for the reasons below.

head: Reason
Explanation
rows: Indians already knew this system: it had worked in India during British rule. K.M. Munshi said: 'Our constitutional traditions have become Parliamentary.'

Ambedkar said a democratic executive needs both stability and responsibility. The American system gives more stability; the British system gives more responsibility. The Draft Constitution preferred more responsibility to more stability.
A young democracy could not risk constant conflict between the legislature and the executive, as happens in the US.
India is a very diverse society. This system lets all sections, interests and regions be represented in the government.

items: A fixed term for the executive that the legislature cannot cut short was NOT a reason for choosing this system. That is a feature of the presidential system.

sections.heading: How India differs from the British model

blocks.text: India's parliamentary system is largely based on the British system, but it is not a replica (exact copy).

head: Aspect
India
Britain
rows: India is a republic: the President is elected, indirectly, by an electoral college.
Britain is a monarchy: the King or Queen gets the post by birth (hereditary).
Parliament is not supreme. Its power is limited by a written Constitution, the federal system, judicial review and Fundamental Rights.
Parliament is sovereign (supreme): courts cannot strike down an Act of Parliament.
Yes. Courts can declare a law void if it violates the Constitution. Questions on whether a constitutional amendment is valid are decided by a Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court.
Can be a member of either House. For example, Indira Gandhi (1966), Deve Gowda (1996) and Manmohan Singh (2004) were members of the Rajya Sabha.
Should be a member of the House of Commons (lower House).
A non-member of Parliament can be a minister for up to six months.
Usually only members of Parliament become ministers.
No legal responsibility. An order of the President does not need to be countersigned (also signed) by a minister, so the minister cannot be held liable for it in court.
Exists. Every public order of the King is countersigned by a minister, and that minister can be held liable in court if the order breaks the law.
The opposition forms a 'shadow cabinet': a team that mirrors the ruling cabinet, keeps a check on it and gets ready to take over as the next government.

items: Features India took from Britain: the cabinet system, collective responsibility, the office of Prime Minister and a bicameral (two-House) legislature. Judicial review is NOT a British feature; Britain does not have it.

blocks.text: see Salient features and sources of the Constitution

sections.heading: Exam traps

items: The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible only to the Lok Sabha (Article 75(3)), not to the Rajya Sabha, even though ministers can be members of either House.
The President is the de jure (nominal) executive. The Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers are the de facto (real) executive. The President is NOT the real head.
The parliamentary system means fusion of powers. India does not have separation of powers in the American sense.
The US President cannot dissolve the House of Representatives, and Congress cannot remove him by a no-confidence vote.
Judicial review, a written Constitution and an elected Head of State make India different from Britain.
Ambedkar: the framers chose more responsibility over more stability. A fixed term for the executive is a presidential feature, not a parliamentary one.

Who said it: 'keystone of the cabinet arch' is Lord Morley; 'sun around which planets revolve' is Ivor Jennings; 'hyphen that joins, buckle that binds' is Walter Bagehot; 'dictatorship of the cabinet' is Ramsay Muir.

In Assertion-Reason questions, a true Reason does not always explain the Assertion. Example: the President is indeed elected indirectly, but that is not why India has a parliamentary system (the reason is that ministers are answerable to the Lok Sabha).
